name: Abihud
title: Descendant of Zerubbabel in the lineage of the Messiah
summary: Abihud is known from the genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew, where he is listed as the son of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim (Matt 1:13). He belongs to the Davidic royal line and forms a central link in the messianic lineage from David to Jesus Christ. Abihud lived in the post-exilic period, when the Jews had returned from Babylon to Judah. Remarkably, he is not mentioned among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chronicles (1 Chron 3:19–20), which has given rise to discussion about his exact familial relationship. Beyond his place in the genealogy, we have no further biblical information about his life, but his role as a bearer of the Davidic promise leading toward the Messiah makes him an important figure in salvation history.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
keyEvents.description: Abihud is listed as the son of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus Christ, showing the messianic line from Abraham through David to Christ.

keyEvents.title: Part of the post-exilic lineage
keyEvents.description: Abihud represents a generation in the period following the return from the Babylonian exile. As a descendant of Zerubbabel, who led Jews back from Babylon to Jerusalem, Abihud belonged to a prominent family that carried forward the royal Davidic heritage during a time when Israel had no kingdom of its own.

keyEvents.title: Link in the messianic lineage
keyEvents.description: Abihud is part of the chain of generations God used to fulfill His promise of a Messiah from David's line. He belongs to the last of three groups of fourteen generations in Matthew's genealogy—from the exile to Christ.

versions.summary: Abihud was a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel and is mentioned in Jesus Christ's genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew. He represents an important link in the messianic lineage from David to Jesus. Little is known about his life beyond his place in the family tree.
versions.title: Descendant of David in the Lineage of the Messiah
versions.reason: [critical] According to Matt 1:13, Abihud is the son of Zerubbabel, not the son of Bela. Bela is a completely different biblical figure (son of Benjamin in Gen 46:21). The father field must be changed to 'Zerubbabel'.; [major] There is no biblical source that refers to Abihud as a 'leader'. He is known only from the genealogy in Matthew 1:13. A more appropriate role would be 'ancestor' or 'forefather in Jesus's lineage'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it should clarify that Abihud is mentioned as the son of Zerubbabel (not Bela) and that he is not listed among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chronicles, which makes his identity disputed.; [minor] Five key events for a person mentioned only in a single verse (Matt 1:13) are excessive. Several of the events overlap and essentially concern the same theme – his place in the genealogy. Consider reducing this to 2–3 events.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For Abihud, there are several interesting points: (1) the name 'Abihud' likely means 'my father is majestic/honorable', (2) Abihud is not listed among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chron 3:19–20, which has led to discussion about whether he might be another name for one of the mentioned sons, or that Matthew uses a different source.

versions.title: Descendant of Zerubbabel in the lineage of the Messiah
versions.reason: [minor] The summary strongly resembles version 1 in the introduction ('Abihud was a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel and is mentioned in Jesus Christ's genealogy in Mat...'). It should be rephrased more distinctly to set it apart from the earlier version.; [minor] The second key event ('Part of the post-exilic lineage') is more contextual background than a specific event directly tied to Abihud himself. This is acceptable given source limitations, but the description could be tightened somewhat.; [minor] The third key event ('Link in God's plan of salvation') cites Matt 1:1 and 1:17, which do not directly mention Abihud. They provide context for the structure of the genealogy but are not direct references to him. It would be better to limit this to verses that actually name him.; [minor] The name explanation is good, but 'hod' (הוֹד) means 'majesty/splendor'. The form 'Abihud' can also be interpreted as 'father of majesty/splendor' rather than 'my father is majestic'. This nuance should be made clearer.

footnotes.text: The name Abihud (אֲבִיהוּד) is composed of the Hebrew words 'av' (אָב, father) and 'hud' (הוּד), a variant of 'hod' (הוֹד, majesty/splendor). The name can be interpreted as 'father of majesty,' 'majesty's father,' or 'my father is majestic.'

Abihud is not listed among Zerubbabel's sons in 1 Chron 3:19–20, where the sons Meshullam and Hananiah are recorded. This has led to various suggestions: Abihud may be an alternative name for one of them, a grandson rather than a son, or Matthew may have followed a different genealogical tradition than that found in the Books of Chronicles.

Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:1–17) is structured into three groups of fourteen generations. Abihud belongs to the third group, from the Babylonian exile to Christ. This symmetrical structure may imply that some links were omitted, which was common practice in ancient Semitic genealogies.

In rabbinic tradition, preserving family lines, especially the Davidic line, was important during the post-exilic period. Although royal rule had ended, descendants of David were regarded as bearers of messianic hope.

Zerubbabel led the first group of Jews returning from Babylon to Jerusalem around 538 BC. He was a Persian-appointed governor in Judah and played a central role in rebuilding the temple. As Abihud's father according to Matthew, this connects Abihud to the leading family in the restored Jewish community.

The difference between the genealogies in Matthew and Luke has been widely discussed. While Matthew traces the lineage from David through Solomon and further through Zerubbabel to Abihud, Luke (Luke 3:27) follows a different line through Nathan, David's son. This highlights that the two evangelists may have had different theological and genealogical perspectives.
